list.listitem: Zika virus is usually transmitted by Aedes species mosquitoes and can cause fever, joint pains or myalgias, conjunctivitis, and/or rash in about 20% of infected individuals. Infection is self-limiting. C
Prevention efforts include avoidance of mosquitoes, eliminating their habitat, wearing light-colored clothing that completely covers the body, and using mosquito repellents. C
The diagnosis is confirmed using polymerase chain reaction (PCR). C
Treatment is primarily supportive. C
The two most serious complications attributed to Zika virus are Guillain–Barré syndrome and microcephaly. C

Zika virus infection is caused by a single-stranded RNA flavivirus. It was first identified in the Zika forest in Uganda in 1947 and is transmitted primarily by the Aedes aegypi and Aedes albopictus species of mosquitoes.

A systematic review evaluated the prevalence of ZIka virus in blood donors. They found that it was highest in French Polynesia from 2013 to 2014 (2.8%), in Brazil from 2015 to 2016 (2.7%), and in Martinique in 2016 (1.8%).
Originally confined to Africa and Southeast Asia, a large outbreak was reported in French Polynesia in 2013. It has since spread to Brazil and has become widespread in Central and South America.

The disease is caused by a virus of the family Flaviviridae and genus Flavivirus. Transmission is via Aedes aegypti mosquito bite, unprotected sex with an infected person, through blood transmission, or through vertical transmission to the fetus.

Zika virus, like its close cousins dengue and chikungunya, is usually transmitted by Aedes species mosquitoes (Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus), which take a blood meal from an infected host and transmit it to another person. In the United States, these mosquitoes are limited to the southeastern states.

The infection may also be sexually transmitted. At the time of writing, little is known about this, but it appears more likely for men to transmit it in semen to female partners. Transmission in utero, perinatally, and via blood products has also been reported, but the extent to which this is a factor in the spread of the disease is unknown.
There is limited evidence that Zika can be transmitted by breastfeeding, although it is not conclusive.

A study of men with symptomatic ZIka virus infection found that they continued to shed viral RNA for up to 6 months or more in some cases, but the viral load declines over time and most documented infections have occurred within 40 days, and usually within 20 days.
There is currently no vaccine for Zika virus, although efforts are underway to develop one. C

A phase 1 trial with 75 participants evaluated a purified inactivated Zika vaccine (ZPIV), following priming with Japanese encephalitis or yellow fever vaccines for one third of particpants each versus no priming. The rate of seroconversion was higher in the non-primed group (88%) than in the primed groups (25% to 32%) but this increased with a 3rd injection and persisted for 2 years. Data regarding effect on preventing infection are still pending. C

The best approach to prevention is avoidance of mosquitoes, eliminating their habitat (mosquitoes can breed in even small amounts of standing water), wearing light-colored clothing that completely covers the body, and using mosquito repellents with DEET and/or mosquito nets. C
DEET appears to be safe in pregnancy, or at least benefits appear to outweigh the harms. C

CDC guidelines recommend that condoms should be worn for at least 90 days after illness onset or travel to an endemic area by the male partner, and 60 days by the female partner (or intercourse should be avoided entirely for that period). B

Protection of houses: a systematic review of studies for other mosquito born diseases found that intradomiciliary residual spraying, insecticide treated nets or curtains, and treatment of larval habitats were most effective. Clean-up campaigns had less effect, and modifications to the house such as plastering the wall had no effect. B
Suspect Zika virus infection in someone who lives in or has recently traveled to an affected area who presents with fever, joint pains or myalgias, conjunctivitis, and/or rash. C
Confirm the diagnosis using PCR. C

list.listitem: Most patients infected with Zika virus (approximately 80%) remain asymptomatic.
When it does cause symptoms, it typically causes acute onset of fever, joint pains, conjunctivitis, headache, myalgias, and a maculopapular rash.
The preferred and most accurate and sensitive test for Zika is PCR.

Tests for Zika-specific IgM antibodies are also available, but may not be positive until the patient has been symptomatic for several days to a week (CDC guidance). An evaluation of 8 commercial IgM and IgG serology tests found very poor sensitivity (6% to 28%) in acute samples, versus 52% to 96% in convalescent serum 7 to 14 days after onset of fever.
A prospective cohort study of 53 participants found that Zika virus RNA was detectable in plasma for 9.9 days, in whole blood for 74 days, and in red blood cells for 95 days.
When suspected based on prenatal ultrasounds, microcephaly was confirmed in 76% of infants and brain abnormalities in 78%.
For pregnant women, the CDC has published guidance for maternal care providers and an algorithm for evaluation. See .
See for the recommended CDC diagnostic strategy for pregnant women with possible exposure to Zika virus infection.
Treatment is primarily supportive. C
Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin until dengue is ruled out as this could exacerbate hemorrhage.
Isolate patients, have them abstain from sexual contact, and assure that they are isolated from mosquitoes.
Treatment is primarily supportive.
Clinical symptoms of Zika virus infection are normally self-limited, lasting a few days to a week. C
The two most serious complications attributed to Zika virus are Guillain–Barré syndrome and microcephaly. B

Guillain–Barré syndrome has been associated with Zika virus infection. Guillain–Barré is an ascending paralysis also associated with other viral infections. Patients may require mechanical ventilation and may be left with permanent sequelae following recovery. A report identified 66 patients with Guillain–Barré following an episode of Zika virus infection, with a mean interval between infection and symptoms of 7 days, range 3 to 10 days.

Zika virus is strongly associated with microcephaly in pregnant women who are infected with Zika, especially early in the first trimester. Microcephaly is a birth defect characterized by incomplete cerebral development and a smaller-than-normal cranium.

Studies of infants with Zika virus infection who were normocephalic at birth show that about 30% have a language delay and 11% a motor delay using the Bayley Scale. However, it is not known how this compares with non-infected infants.
A 3 year Brazilian cohort study found that mortality in infants with congenital Zika virus infection is about 10 times higher than non-infected infants (53 vs 5.6 deaths/1000 live births).

Zika virus infection in pregnant women is strongly associated with microcephaly. Women who are pregnant and living in an area where the disease is endemic should take great care to avoid mosquito bites, wear protective clothing, and use strict environmental controls and procedures to minimize mosquito breeding indoors and outdoors.

Congenital Zika syndrome consists of microcephaly, low birth weight for gestational age, parenchymal calcifications, ventriculomegaly, hypoplasia or atrophy of the CNS, arthrogryposis, and visual problems. A systematic review of 46 studies found that the clinical signs seen most frequently were microcephaly (45% of studies), hypertonicity (17%), seizures (15%) and abnormal crying and irritability early in life (13%). The odds ratio of Zika infection during pregnancy for microcephaly was 56, and for intrauterine fetal death was 4.0.
The risk of microcephaly was somewhat higher in male infants (RR 1.3), first trimester infection (RR 1.4) and symptomatic infection (RR 1.5).

A systematic review of 108 studies with 24,699 completed Zika-affected pregnancies found that non-fatal adverse outcomes such as microcephaly occured in a median of 5.9% of pregnancies, and fetal death 6.3%.
It is uncertain whether Zika can be transmitted in breastmilk. A systematic review found that while uncommon, it was detectable in some breast milk samples.
